full_judgment:
2. Appellant (Jashimuddin Kanchan) and respondent (Ali Ashraf) both purchased the same land at about the same time from two rival owners under registered kabalas and thereby entered into the litigation. The land in question measures .05 acre out of 37 acre in plot No. 460 of Khatian No. 127 of Mouza Misri, Laksham. The land originally be-longed to one Badsha Mia, who by an Ijara kabuliyat dated 23 June 1926 leased it to Ram Prosad Muchi, a cobbler by profession, for a period of 5 years at a yearly rent of Tk. 4/- Badsha Mia then exchanged his entire property including the suit land with Mohesh Chandra Saha by a registered deed of exchange dated 16 October 1936. At the time of the exchange Ram Prosad Muchi was continuing in possession of the suit land by holding over under the Ijara kabuliyat. Ram Prosad Muchi continued even after this ex-change, but controversy arose since then. 

 4. The appellant, on the other hand, claimed that by the "Ijara kabuliyat" dated 23.6.26 (Ext .8) no Darrayati interest was created in favour of Ram Prosad Muchi, that he did not get any other tenancy right but was a mere Ijaradar for a short time, that though he continued as Ijaradar at the time of the exchange of the suit land, he some time after the ex-change, left the suit land and surrendered his possession to the new landlord, Mohesh Chandra Saha and permanently settled at Daulatganj Bazar where he died. Upon surrender of the land by Ram Prosad Muchi, the landlord Mohesh Saha entered upon and possessed it as khas land and on his his death, his son, Upendra Saha, inherited and possessed it and then, by the registered kabala dated 7 May 1977, as already referred to, transferred it to him (appellant) and delivered its possession. He further alleged that the respondent traced out Ram Prosad's sons, who were residing at Daulatganj and obtained from them a fraudulent kabala, Ext. 1, as already referred to, and threatened him with dispossession. Thereupon he filed an application under section 145 CrPC (Misc. Case No. 34 of 1977) before the Sub-divisional Magistrate, Comilla, who started a proceeding there-on, attached the land and appointed the Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station as its receiver. The respondent challenged the order of attachment by Criminal Motion No. 361 of 1977 but it was rejected by the Sessions Judge. Thereupon the respondent took law in has own hand and dispossessed him (appellant) from a part of the suit land forcibly erecting three huts and cutting away two Mango trees. In the circumstances, he filed Title Suit No. 293 of 1977 in the same court of Munsif praying for declaration of his title to the entire suit land measuring .05 acre and recovery of possession in respect of 0.01 of the suit land. 

 5. Both the suits were tried on analogous basis by the Munsif, who by his judgment dated 29 December 1980, dismissed the respondent's suit (Title Suit No. 223 of 1977) and decreed the appellant's suit (Title Suit No. 293 of 1977) upon findings, among other things, that by the Ijara kabuliyat Ram Prosad Muchi did not acquire any Darrayati right, that whatever right he got he surrendered it to the landlord and left the place for good and as such his sons inherited nothing to transfer. Respondent preferred appeals in both the suits, Title Appeal No. 36 of 1981 in respect of TS 223 of 1977 and Title Appeal 37 of 1981 in respect of TS No. 293 of 1977. Both the appeals were disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge by a common judgment dated 21 November 1982. Both the appeals were dismissed; but in the case of TA No. 37 of 1981, the decree was conditional, that is, the plaintiff of the suit (appellant) was found to have been dispossessed from the entire suit land and not from the area of .01 acre and as such he was advised to amend his plaint paying ad valorem Court fee to seek possession of the entire suit land. (0.5 acre) within 15 days failing which his suit "would stand dismissed". In compliance with this advice of the court he amended the plaint on payment of the necessary Court fee, and consequently, the suit was decreed finally on 30.12.82. 

 10. Mr. MH Khandkar has referred to the "Ijara " kabuliyat (Ext. 8) of the year 1926; executed by Ram Pros ad Muchi, He contends that by this kabuliyat only "ijara right" or temporary lease was created but no tenancy was created. 'Ijara', he contends, means a "farming lease" for a temporary period without right of renewal. In support, he has referred to SN Bose's Legal Dictionary. There is no dispute that an ijara right is not a tenancy right and under an "Ijara" kabuliyat no tenancy is created. But the matter may be different if the ijara right is renewed and the Ijara holder continues in possession for an indefinite period. The Ijara in question was created in 1926 by the original owner Badsha Mia for a period of five years, on expiration of this period the Ijara-holder is found to have continued when the land was exchanged with Mohesh Saha in 1936, and even after the exchange, he is found to have continued in possession of the land for a few years more. For realisation of arrear rent Mohesh Chandra Saha filed a rent suit as appears from the papers Ext. 5 series. These papers show that Ram Prosad Muchi, the original Ijaradar was in possession of the land upto 1345 BS.corresponding to 1938-39 AD. Appellant challenged Ext. 5 series as fabricated documents but did not produce any evidence in support of his contention. The Ijara Kabuliyat (Ext. 8), read with the Papers-Ext. 5 series, show that though initially an ijara-or temporary lease-was intended, it ripened into some sort of under-tenancy because of continuous possession, and as the land was used for non-agricultural purpose e.g. as a residential hut, it was governed by the Transfer of Property Act at that time. As to whether Ram Prosad Muchi continued in possession after 1938-39 to 1949 and also thereafter till April 1956, parties came up with diametrically opposite versions. Appellant alleged that Ram Prosad left the place for good and established himself in a different place, Daulatgonj Bazar, and lived there permanently till his death; respondent, on the other hand, alleged that Ram Prosad continued all along in the suit land till 1956 on payment of rent to the landlord and then became a tenant under the Government on wholesale acquisition of all rent receiving interests. I shall consider these two conflicting claims in due course, but now I shall see the legal position of Ram Prosad Muchi till 1938-1939. 

 11. As indicated above, prior to the coming into force of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, with effect from 20 October 1949, tenancy right in a non-agricultural land was governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1982. So from 1926 to1939 Ram Prosad Muchi's position was that of a tenant at will; his interest in the suit land was not transferable, nor heritable, nor was it capable of being bequeathed. Such rights were conferred on a non- agricultural tenant, for the first time, under section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949; under this section certain classes of persons holding non-agricultural land by lease were given non-ejectable right. Ram Prosad Muchi, in view of his Ijara kabuliyat followed by continuous possession, might fall into one such class under section 7(4) if he had the required period of possession. That is, if Ram Pro sad were to acquire these rights under this section it must be shown that he had continued in possession of the suit land for a period of twelve years prior to October, 1949. But since 1938-39, as appears, there is no reliable evidence that he possessed the land excepting the rent-receipts Ext. 2 series. These rent- receipts relate to a few years preceding the year 1955- 56. These rent-receipts have been seriously challenged by the appellant as false and fabricated and his contention is that Ram Pro sad abandoned the suit land, where he had only a dwelling hut, and permanently resided in Daulatgonj Bazar. Respondent remains silent about this change of residence of Ram Prosad, but his son, PW 2 and one of the executants of the kabala Ext. 1 dated 30 March 1977, admitted that he had been residing in Daulatganj for 20-25 years as against the appellant's assertion that the family of PW 2 had been residing in Daulatpur permanently for 25-30 years. This period, if correct, would take Ram Prosad's family to Daulatganj near about the year 1947-48. That is if Ram Prosad had left the suitland before 1949 he did not acquire the non-ejectable right under section 7, with the result that his sons would acquire no interest in the suit land for subsequent transfer under the kabala Ext. 1. In other words, he would have no tenancy right which his sons would inherit and on the basis of which they would become tenants under the Government on wholesale acquisition of rent-receiving interest in 1956. Decisions of the then Dhaka High Court on this point have been reported in Nihar Ranjan Vs. Nurannessa Chowdhury 10 DLR 472 and Delbaz Vs. Saroda Sundar; Debya 13 DLR 334. The Ijara lease was taken by Ram Prosad in the year 1926, but the land was transferred by his sons in 1977. There is no evidence when he died except the disputed rent-receipts, Ext. 2 series, which were allegedly granted by Ram Prosad in the years nearing 1956. In the case of his death occurring prior to 1949 his sons inherited nothing; The rent-receipts show that the suit land was treated as an agricultural land whereas it is a non-agricultural land used for residential purpose only. It is these rent-receipts on which the respondent's whole case depends.
